text: i can still remember that tragic day as if it happened yesterday, and even now, the pain of it stays with me. we were at buguey beach with two of our staff members. it was supposed to be a simple stopover, just a chance to relax for a while. one of our staff decided to go into the water. three stayed on the shore , watching him. he was only about a meter away from the children playing near the sand, and from where i stood, the water looked shallow, no more than knee-deep. then everything changed in an instant. a large wave suddenly hit him. i heard him call out for help, and before we could react, another wave came. he tried a third time to jump up and call for help, but after that, we could no longer see him. the waves just kept coming. we immediately called for the lifeguard, but he was unable to reach him in time. rescuers from the mdrrmo arrived quickly with a life buoy and did everything they could, but they could not save him. divers from santa ana, cagayan were also called, but they were nearly two hours away. by then, what started as a rescue effort had sadly became a retrieval operation. his body was recovered the following day. those hours of waiting were some of the hardest moments. i remember staring at the water, praying, crying, and asking myself over and over how something so terrible could happen so fast. one moment we were all together, and the next, he was gone. the next hard thing is to call his family hoping what just happened was a nightmare.. for a long time, i carried so many questions and so much guilt. i kept wondering if there was something more i could have done. even today, whenever i hear about similar incidents, it brings me right back to that day and the heartbreak we experienced. it is a pain i would never wish on anyone. more than anything, i hope no family ever has to endure that kind of loss. prayers for healing on both side. :red_heart:

text: negligence! even if they had been doing this activity for the past 10 years, that does not automatically make it safe. if the area is known for strong waves, rip currents, or dangerous open-water conditions, then continuing to bring students there is like saying, “let’s see if fire can actually burn.” that is not experience. that is complacency. at some point, if you keep ignoring obvious risks, it stops looking like an accident and starts looking like a failure of basic judgment. as if the coaching staff have a foresight of a potato. i feel bad for all the students involved because the adults failed them. if you are bringing young people into the freaking pacific ocean, there should have been proper safeguards: lifeguards on standby, flotation devices, rescue boats or personnel nearby, emergency medical support, and a clear rescue plan. may briefing kayo about ripcurrents tapos rescue plan at floatters wala? this is what makes it so painful. it feels preventable. these are still kids. realistically, many students will just follow instructions, trust the adults, and go with the flow. they may not feel comfortable questioning a coach, a school authority, or a group activity, especially in a culture where speaking up can easily be seen as being difficult. that is why adult responsibility matters even more. i also wonder if parents were clearly informed about the exact activities planned. if more parents had known the full details, maybe more people would have asked the right questions: is this safe? what are the risks? are there lifeguards? are there flotation devices? what happens if someone gets swept away? sometimes, more eyes mean more foresight. and in this case, that kind of foresight could have mattered. and yes, it is also sad to see other students being bashed, because they are also traumatized. but the pain of rene and divine’s families should not be minimized either. two young lives were lost. if the typical filipino is mad about this news, ano pa yung mga bata na nakita na inaahon yung teammates nila? it's exhausting to see this news on my fyp, but i hope we don't forget it and really push for accountability.
